summary: Psalm 131 is a brief Song of Ascents associated in its heading with David. The speaker denies pride and restless ambition, describes a deliberately quieted soul with the image of a weaned child resting with its mother, and then turns outward to call Israel to hope in Yahweh forever.
whyItMatters: Within Book V and the Songs of Ascents, this psalm gives pilgrimage prayer a posture of humility, restraint, and trust. It shows confidence in God not as loud certainty, but as a settled refusal to grasp at matters beyond the speaker.

context.author: The heading says, “By David,” but Psalms headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging; readers differ on how much the heading establishes historically.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the psalm as prayer.
context.date: The psalm belongs to the collected Psalter, an anthology formed over time; its precise date is uncertain.
context.setting: A Song of Ascents within Book V, a group of psalms associated with ascent or pilgrimage language; the chapter itself speaks from an interior posture and then addresses Israel.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry and prayer, moving from first-person humility to a communal summons.

outline.heading: A heart kept low
outline.note: The speaker addresses Yahweh and rejects arrogance, lofty eyes, and preoccupation with matters too great or wonderful.

outline.heading: A quieted soul
outline.note: The speaker describes inward stillness through the image of a weaned child with its mother.

outline.heading: Israel called to hope
outline.note: The psalm turns from the individual speaker to Israel and calls the community to hope in Yahweh without end.

keyVerses.text: A Song of Ascents. By David. Yahweh, my heart isn’t arrogant, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me.
keyVerses.why: This opening names the psalm’s heading and sets its central posture: the speaker refuses pride and the grasping after matters beyond him.

keyVerses.text: Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.
keyVerses.why: This is the psalm’s central image, explaining humility not as self-contempt but as a quieted inner life.

keyVerses.text: Israel, hope in Yahweh, from this time forward and forever more.
keyVerses.why: The closing line expands the speaker’s personal posture into an address to the whole community.

themes: trust pictured as a weaned child

questions.question: What is a “Song of Ascents”?
questions.answer: The heading places Psalm 131 among the Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120–134. These poems include songs of journeying to Yahweh’s house and worshiping there, but the heading does not establish this psalm’s exact original occasion. Here it introduces a short prayer about humility, quietness, and hope.

questions.question: Does “By David” prove David personally wrote this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading associates the psalm with David. Such headings are ancient parts of the Psalter, and the Hebrew construction can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging. The traditional reading takes it as a byline; a broader Davidic association is also possible. The heading alone does not settle the poem’s authorship.

questions.question: What attitude does the speaker reject in verse 1?
questions.answer: The speaker says his heart is not arrogant and his eyes are not lofty. He also says he does not concern himself with “great matters” or “things too wonderful” for him. The verse presents humility as accepting human limits before Yahweh.

questions.question: Are “great matters” bad in this psalm?
questions.answer: The psalm does not say that great matters are evil. It says the speaker does not occupy himself with matters too great or wonderful for him. The focus is on refusing proud overreach, not on rejecting thought, responsibility, or wonder.

questions.question: What does the image of a weaned child mean here?
questions.answer: Verse 2 compares the speaker’s soul to “a weaned child with his mother.” A weaned child is not pictured as grabbing for milk, but as resting near the mother. The image communicates calm, dependence, and settled trust.

questions.question: What does it mean that the speaker has “stilled and quieted” his soul?
questions.answer: The line describes an inward state the speaker has intentionally brought about. The psalm does not give a technique or a backstory; it simply depicts a soul no longer restless before God. The repeated child image makes the quietness concrete rather than abstract.

questions.question: Why does the psalm shift from “my soul” to “Israel”?
questions.answer: The first two verses are personal, but the final verse addresses the whole people. The speaker’s quiet trust becomes a communal invitation: “Israel, hope in Yahweh.” The psalm moves from individual humility to shared hope.

questions.question: Is this psalm telling readers never to ask hard questions?
questions.answer: No. The Psalter includes protest, confusion, confession, and unanswered lament elsewhere, so this short psalm should not be used to silence every hard question. Psalm 131 speaks specifically about arrogance, lofty eyes, and grasping after matters beyond the speaker, then offers quiet trust as its answer.

questions.question: What kind of hope does the final verse call for?
questions.answer: The final verse calls Israel to hope “in Yahweh.” Its time horizon is open-ended: “from this time forward and forever more.” The verse does not describe the circumstances of that hope, but it anchors the community’s future-facing trust in Yahweh.

glossary.def: A heading attached to this psalm; it identifies the psalm as part of a titled group without explaining the full setting inside the verse itself.
In this verse, the speaker’s inner posture before Yahweh; it is described as not arrogant.
A phrase in verse 1 for a proud or elevated stance; it parallels the speaker’s denial of an arrogant heart.
The central image in verse 2, picturing a child resting with its mother and helping describe the speaker’s quieted soul.
The action Israel is called to in verse 3: trusting Yahweh from now onward.
